title: Seven, and Nobody Agrees
logline: Seven colossal figures cut in relief out of one rock face in low scrub country, with a standing Buddha thirteen metres high in the middle, where the count is the only thing that has never been disputed: not one of the names is more than a proposal, the proposed dates span five centuries, and no ancient text mentions the place at all.
human_question: If the only certain thing about something is how many of it there are, what exactly am I holding when I use its name?

place.what_kind_of_place: A long, low outcrop of rock standing out of dry thorn scrub in the island's south-eastern interior, at the foot of the highlands, with seven figures cut in relief out of one face of it. The middle figure is a standing Buddha about thirteen metres high, reported as the tallest standing Buddha figure on the island; three more stand on either side of it, between about six and seven and a half metres each. None of them was ever separated from the rock; they are still the rock, cut back. A shallow tank lies close by with dead trees standing in the water, and the foundations of a ruined monastery with a small brick stupa lie about half a kilometre away in the scrub. It is a working place of worship with a caretaker, offerings at the foot of the central figure, and a modest number of visitors on an ordinary day rather than a crowd.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Three things carry it with the sound off. The scale, which needs no explanation at all: a person standing at the foot of the central figure reaches about a fifth of the way up its robe, and there is nothing else in the frame to measure against. The arrival of the light, on a wall reported to face east, when the sun comes in low and almost flat along the rock and seven bodies lift out of what was a single grey mass a few minutes earlier. And what is left of the paint: patches of stucco still stuck to the robe, one long streak of orange running down it, and one of the six flanking figures still holding much of its white finish. Around all of it, from the air, is scrub country with nothing else in it. No town, no second monument, no crowd. Seven giants in thorn.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Almost nothing here is under the crew's control and almost all of it is light. The relief exists for about the first hour of the day and then flattens as the sun climbs, until by mid-morning the same wall is a pale shadowless surface and the figures have gone half flat. In the afternoon the face sits in its own shade and the modelling comes back, cooler and softer. Rain darkens the rock and brings the orange up. On the tank, birds work the shallows among the dead trees all day. At the base, flowers are laid and cleared, a lamp is lit and goes out, and swept ground is swept again.
place.when_it_looks_best: The dry months, roughly December to April, for the light and because the last few kilometres in are partly unsealed. The first hour after sunrise is the whole film, if the reported east orientation holds: that is when the carving has depth. Late afternoon is the second window, with the wall in its own shade and a bright sky above the top of the rock. The hour after rain is the best the colour will ever look. Poya days and festival days are the wrong days to film here.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A dawn film about seven giants in a thorn wilderness. It opens in the dark on water with dead trees standing in it, moves up to a grey wall where something enormous is only just legible, and then the sun arrives and seven figures come out of the stone. It goes close — plaster, a streak of orange, a hand held up in a gesture more than a thousand years old, a hollow cut at the base that is always wet — and then pulls all the way back to one frame holding every figure and one small person at the foot of the biggest. Beginning, middle, payoff. A viewer who never hears a word of narration gets all of it.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same footage becomes a demonstration of the difference between counting something and naming it. The voice does only two things. It counts, which anyone watching can check: seven, six and one. And it reports, attaching every name and every date to whoever proposed it — Paranavitana, Dohanian, Wickramagamage, Bell — so that an identification and a proposer arrive in the same breath, every time, and the viewer is never handed a fact the stone does not carry. Against that, the compendium's own habit: five aggregates, twelve bases, eighteen elements, four truths, exact numbers the manual argues for and will not let anyone round off, each taught for a stated purpose. Here is a numbered list carved forty feet high whose count has held for more than a thousand years and whose members have no names of their own. Nothing needs explaining. The voice only has to be honest about which half of each sentence is certain.

sequence.on_screen: Before sunrise. Low over grey-green thorn scrub and a shallow tank with dead trees standing in the water, birds lifting off it. Ahead, the rock: one long mass, still flat, with shapes in it that cannot yet be separated from it.
sequence.voice: Somebody organised this. Seven figures, cut out of one face of rock, the middle one more than forty feet high. And then nothing was written down. No chronicle mentions this rock. Nothing carved on it gives a name to anything on it, and its own old name is not known. Every name and every date you are about to hear was proposed by somebody standing where you are standing, a thousand years late.

sequence.on_screen: First sun, coming in low and almost flat along the wall. One static wide frame from the ground, the whole face in it, air above the head of the central figure: six standing figures and one in the middle, lifting out of the rock as the light rakes across them.
sequence.voice: Count them. Six, and one in the middle. Seven. That number is the only thing about this rock that nobody has ever disputed.

sequence.on_screen: The central figure from low down: the robe with patches of stucco still gripping it and a long streak of orange running down the stone. Closer on the streak, then on the raised right hand.
sequence.voice: The robe was plastered and painted, and what is left of the colour is one long streak of orange. Whoever paid for this meant it to be splendid, and the old manual is oddly firm about that sort of thing: whether something is fine or foul is not simply decided by whoever happens to be looking. What nobody can do is watch the centuries go past. The Pradeepika says you never see ageing itself. You know how high the flood came from the mark it left on the wall.

sequence.on_screen: The three figures on the Buddha's right, in warm early light: the tall one still holding much of its white finish; beside it a female figure standing with her weight thrown into one hip; then the third.
sequence.voice: The tall one with the white paint on it is thought to be the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara. The figure beside him, standing in the thrice-bent posture, is thought to be Tārā. Thought to be. The third has been called Sudhanakumāra, and Mañjuśrī, and Vishnu, and Brahmā. In 1916 H. C. P. Bell looked at these same three and read them as a prince, a queen and a brahmin out of a birth story instead.

sequence.on_screen: The three on the other side: a crowned figure, one holding a small hourglass-shaped object, and a last figure with nothing in its hands. Then the flame-shaped hollow cut into the rock at the base, wet, with a dark stain running out of it.
sequence.voice: On this side, a crowned figure usually called Maitreya, the Buddha who has not arrived yet; one holding a vajra; and one nobody has named at all. Senarath Paranavitana thought the great figure in the middle was not the Buddha of our era either, but Dīpaṅkara, the one tradition credits with the prediction. The hollow at the bottom of the rock is always wet, and nobody has explained that either. This complex belongs to the Mahāyāna school, which is the one thing here everybody agrees about and the one thing this film is not qualified to explain.

sequence.on_screen: The payoff, with the light still low. Starting tight on the figure nobody has named, the camera pulls steadily back, flat on to the wall, until all seven are in one frame with a single person standing at the foot of the central figure — the only measure of size anywhere in the shot — and scrub country running out behind to nothing.
sequence.voice: Five centuries of proposals for when this was made. Paranavitana said the late fifth. Professor Dohanian said the second half of the seventh. Professor Wickramagamage said the ninth. Other accounts say the tenth. There is no text to check any of it against, so the dating is done on style: on how the stone is cut. What you can do from here, knowing nothing, is count. Seven.

sequence.on_screen: Late in the day. The wall in its own shade; flowers and a lamp on the ledge at the foot of the central figure and the swept ground in front of it. Then, half a kilometre off in the scrub, low foundations and a small brick stupa, and the tank going quiet.
sequence.voice: The manual this voice keeps quoting counts things for a living. Five. Twelve. Eighteen. Four. Each list has an exact number and the book argues for why it is not one more or one fewer, and it says plainly what the counting is for: not an inventory, and not to prove that nobody is there. It is to loosen the grip of this is me, this is mine. Seven figures. The count holds. Everything else on this rock is somebody's proposal, including the ones we just made.

concept_merge.why_together: C077 is not a doctrine here, it is a practice: the compendium sets out what there is as numbered lists, and the number in each one is argued for rather than approximate. The Pradeepika gives the order of the five and the reason there are exactly five, neither fewer nor more [C077-P:L982–L984; C077-P:L996–L998], the twelve bases as six doors each paired with its own object [C077-P:L1315; C077-M:L47], and the eighteen elements, whose membership is identical in both books although the two set them out in different orders [C077-P:L1431–L1439; C077-M:L54]. It also states the point of all the counting: not tidiness, but loosening the habit of saying I and mine [C077-P:L1006–L1010; C077-M:L24], and the closing passage says the four sortings exist at all because people are confused about name, or about form, or about both [C077-P:L3023–L3031]. So the count is fixed and purposeful, and the names are carefully glossed: an element is 'without a being, without a living soul' [C077-P:L1447]. C084 supplies the other half. A concept is both what is made known and what makes it known [C084-P:L25]; the meaning-concepts include the whole made of parts, the shape and the being [C084-P:L27–L41]; and the spoken sound of a name is ultimately real while the name it carries is not, living instead in whoever receives it [C084-P:L47; C084-M:L21]. Seven figures cut out of one rock face put both at once in front of a camera. The count is checkable by anyone who looks. Every name laid over the seven was supplied from outside, centuries later, by people who left their own names attached to their proposals while the figures kept none.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That a count and a name are different kinds of thing, and that most of what we believe we know about something is the name layer. C077 alone would be a lesson in lists. C084 alone would make this a film about scholarly caution. Together they produce the one frame the film exists for: all seven in the low light, with a person at the foot of the tallest, in which the number is exactly legible and not one name is. The pairing also protects the film from two easy endings. It cannot conclude that the figures are 'only stone', because the sources keep conventional wholes valid in their own domain and keep the colour, the hardness and the seeing fully real; and it cannot conclude that nobody is there, because C077's whole analysis is aimed at grasping rather than at existence [C077-P:L996–L998], and states elsewhere that there is suffering without a separate sufferer standing behind it, which is a claim about ownership and never a licence to make light of anyone [C077-P:L2292–L2298].

concept_links.why: The digest's compendium is the practice of setting out what there is as a numbered list with a purpose: the five in their order and the argument for exactly five [C077-P:L982–L984; C077-P:L996–L998], the twelve bases as six doors each with its own object [C077-P:L1315; C077-M:L47], the eighteen elements with identical membership in the two books and a different arrangement in each [C077-P:L1431–L1439; C077-M:L54], and the four truths. The word for a division means a collection, and the Pradeepika explicitly sets aside the sense in which the same word would be a mere designation [C077-P:L36–L42], which is the distinction this location is standing on: what is gathered and counted, as against what is called something. The stated purpose governs the whole film — the counting is to loosen 'this is me, this is mine' [C077-P:L1006–L1010; C077-M:L24], and the sortings exist because people are confused about name, form, or both [C077-P:L3023–L3031]; the elements in particular are taught for those who take awareness itself to be a self [C077-P:L1853; C077-M:L60], and the gloss for an element is 'without a being, without a living soul' [C077-P:L1447]. Beat 3 comes straight out of the digest as well: ageing cannot be watched, only read off the mark it leaves, the way a flood is read off a wall [C077-P:L2547–L2560], which is exactly what dating by style is. Three of the digest's does_not_transfer lines are load-bearing and are written into the risks: the analysis must never become 'you do not exist' or a denial of responsibility, because what it takes apart is the grasping 'this is me, this is mine' [C077-P:L996–L998; C077-M:L24]; 'beauty is in the eye of the beholder' is the reverse of what the source says, since desirability is fixed by the result-consciousness and 'cannot be deceived' [C077-P:L193–L201], which is why beat 3 credits the makers with meaning it to be splendid; and 'no self, so no one really suffers' reverses the teaching, which says suffering exists and only a separate owner of it is missing [C077-P:L2292–L2298]. One further limit keeps the film honest about its own conceit: the sources' sub-counts follow conventions rather than arithmetic, and the Pradeepika counts the same mind-object base as sixty-nine items in one place and as twenty in another [C077-P:L1409; C077-P:L1865], so the voice may say that each list has an exact number argued for, and must not claim that every number in the books is stable.

What the scholars did at this rock is the digest's subject in its plainest form. A concept is both what is made known and the means of making it known [C084-P:L25], and the sources sort the meaning-concepts — the whole made of parts, the shape, the being, the direction, the time [C084-P:L27–L41; C084-M:L9; C084-M:L11–L19] — apart from the names that convey them. A figure in relief is a configuration of rock that was never separated from the rock, so the name laid over it is doing all the work of telling you what it is. The Margaya's separation of the spoken sound, which is ultimately real, from the name it carries, which is not and which comes up in whoever receives it [C084-M:L21; C084-P:L47], is precisely what happens when a modern voice says 'Tārā' over a carving that carries no name of its own, and the sixfold scheme of how a name stands to its basis, according to whether name and basis are ultimately there [C084-P:L49–L71; C084-M:L23–L35], is the frame for a dispute in which the carvings are certainly present and the proposed identities are proposals. The digest's three limits are absolute here and appear in the risks: the existent and non-existent pairs are technical categories and not a scheme of true and false; 'language constructs reality' or 'nothing is real' overreaches a source that keeps sound, colour and mind fully real and conventional wholes valid in their own domain; and a film must never tell a participant that the name they use is wrong, which at a living place of worship rules out any suggestion that the people who come here are praying to the wrong figure. The division test — cloth pulled apart into thread [C084-M:L7] — is deliberately kept out of the narration, because at a place of worship it would read as debunking rather than as analysis.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That counting something and naming it are two different operations, and that most of what we think we know about a thing sits in the second one. Seven figures have stood in the open for more than a thousand years. The number has never been in doubt; the names, the century, even which of them is the Buddha of this era have all been argued, and the arguments are recent. A viewer can check the count from a single frame and cannot check anything else, which is the whole demonstration.
what_must_be_real: The disagreement, reported as a disagreement. Every identification spoken in the film carries the person who proposed it, no proposal is presented as settled, and the film never chooses between them, on screen or in narration. It does not explain the figures doctrinally: the series' sources are Theravāda Abhidhamma manuals and they have nothing to say about who these figures are, and the film says so rather than borrowing authority it does not have. The complex's Mahāyāna character is stated as a fact of the site and is never ranked against anything. This is a living place of worship: no act of worship is interrupted, restarted, moved or lit for filming, nobody is filmed who cannot meaningfully refuse, and nobody in frame is presented as devout, awed or attained. The person who gives the scale in the payoff shot is there by prior agreement and is not a worshipper caught in the frame; if the shot cannot be got that way, it is got with a member of the crew or not at all. The local account of the oil in the hollow, the treasure chamber and the broken nose are reported as local accounts if they are used at all, never as history. Measurements are given with a source or not given, because published heights for the central figure differ by three metres. No paint, plaster or carving is touched, cleaned, wetted or lit from close range.
position_hint: middle of the group: it needs the opening film's separation of a name from the thing it names already in the viewer's hand, and it earns its place by turning that separation on something nobody can settle, then leaving one exact number standing where all the names failed. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Resolving the dispute. Any framing, caption, cutaway or line that lets one identification read as the correct one destroys the subject; the disagreement is the film.

Explaining the figures doctrinally. The film's sources are Theravāda Abhidhamma manuals with nothing to say about who these figures are, and a voice that starts describing what a bodhisattva is for would both overreach the sources and imply the identification is settled.

Ranking traditions. A Mahāyāna complex in a largely Theravāda country must be recorded as a layer of history, never adjudicated, never presented as heterodox, a curiosity or a survival, and never used to set one school above another.
Telling anyone their name for a figure is wrong. The C084 digest forbids it outright, and the people who bring flowers here use names.

Overreaching into 'nothing is real' or 'it is only stone'. The sources keep colour, sound, hardness and mind fully real and keep conventional wholes valid in their own domain, and at a place of worship this reading would land as debunking.

Letting the analysis become 'nobody is there'. The C077 digest says the taking-apart is aimed at the grasping 'this is me, this is mine', not at a person's existence, and that there is suffering without a separate owner of it — which is never a licence to make light of anyone in front of the camera.
Saying, or implying, that the figures are only fine because people agree they are; the digest says the sources hold the opposite, and beat 3 is written to credit the makers instead.

Restaging the opening film's payoff. A shape made of nothing belongs to the mountain and its shadow; this film's subject is an exact count with unnameable members, and the shape-concept stays in the notes.
Treating the mustard-oil hollow, the treasure legend or the broken nose as fact, or letting the film drift into a mystery-of-the-ancients register that the site's real uncertainty does not need.
Quoting a height as fact. Published figures for the central image run from 42 ft 8 in and 13 m through 15.5 m to 16 m and 51 ft, and the file pages of the reference photographs themselves say 16 m.

Claiming the sources' numbers are all stable in order to sharpen the contrast; the Pradeepika's own sub-counts follow different conventions, counting the same mind-object base as sixty-nine items in one place and as twenty in another [C077-P:L1409; C077-P:L1865].

Drone permission over a gazetted protected monument, which needs the Department of Archaeology's no-objection letter, Ministry of Defence security clearance and Civil Aviation Authority approval, and may simply be refused. The film has to work from the ground, and a thirteen-metre figure supplies its own scale against a person standing at its foot.

The payoff depends on low light on a face reported to be east-facing. If the orientation is wrong or the morning is flat, the relief does not separate from the rock and there is no second attempt that day.
Filming worship as spectacle, or using the caretaker as a scale figure or an informant without consent given in advance and understood.
drop_if: Filming cannot happen without interrupting worship, or without filming people who cannot meaningfully refuse.
Access is only granted on condition that the film adopts the site's own labelling of the figures as fact.
The count itself turns out to be disputed in the current archaeological record, which would remove the one certainty the film is built on.
The only usable framings of the figures require lighting, cleaning or otherwise touching the carved surface.

connections.note: Four living names for one mountain, all in everyday use and none of them wrong, against seven carvings whose names are all recent proposals by scholars and whose count is the only settled thing about them.
A name whose animal was never an animal, and figures that never had names at all; both sites have had names supplied to them by visitors for centuries, and this one keeps the number instead.
One name laid over an enormous number of identical units, and an exact, small number of figures with no names of their own. Deliberately kept apart: nothing here is built on heaps, units or donors.

selection.reason: It is the only candidate in the group where the compendium's own practice of exact enumeration is physically present at cinema scale and where the count is the single undisputed fact on the site, and it replaces a gem-washing film that duplicated another candidate's archetype.

review.note: Rewritten onto a new location and a new subject. The hand-worked gem field is gone: it was one of two gem-washing films in this group and was set aside, and the film that stood on it went with it. The place is now a rock face in the south-eastern scrub country with seven colossal figures cut in relief out of it, dominated by a standing Buddha of about thirteen metres, reported as the tallest standing Buddha figure on the island, with traces of its stuccoed robe and a long streak of orange paint still on it. The historical binding is that almost nothing about the site is settled and the count is the exception: no ancient text mentions the place, its original name is unknown, nothing carved on it names anything on it, and so every identification is a modern proposal — the central figure of one triad thought to be Avalokiteśvara, a female figure in the thrice-bent posture thought to be Tārā, a third variously proposed as Sudhanakumāra, Mañjuśrī, Vishnu or Brahmā, a crowned figure usually called Maitreya, one holding a vajra, one nobody names, and Paranavitana's proposal that the central Buddha is Dīpaṅkara rather than Śākyamuni, with H. C. P. Bell in 1916 reading the whole group as a birth story instead. The proposed dates span five centuries: Paranavitana the late fifth, Dohanian the later seventh, Wickramagamage the ninth, other accounts the tenth, all of it resting on style because there is no text to check. That is why it binds to C077, which is read fresh here not as a doctrine but as the practice of setting out what there is as numbered lists whose counts are argued for and whose purpose is stated: here is a numbered list carved forty feet high, complete in its count and unnameable in its members. C084 supplies the name laid over a form and the difference between what is made known and what makes it known. New title, place block, two-layer test, seven-beat sequence with both concept links re-tested against the digests, a historical_thread that keeps what is certain and what is disputed apart, and a risks list carrying the digests' load-bearing limits: that the analysis must not become 'you do not exist', that desirability is not simply relative to the beholder, that nobody may be told their name for a figure is wrong, and that a Mahāyāna site in a largely Theravāda country is recorded as a layer and never ranked or explained doctrinally. Kept clear of the group's neighbours: it is not four living names for one mountain, not a donor's name outliving its person, and not one name over a heap of units.

suggested_location.name: Buduruwagala rock-cut figures (Buduruwagala Raja Maha Viharaya)

also_known_as.name: Buduruwagala
also_known_as.meaning: the rock of Buddha images, from budu (Buddha), ruva (image) and gala (rock)
also_known_as.used_by: the modern Sinhala name; the site's ancient name is not known

suggested_location.region: Monaragala District, Uva Province: low dry-zone scrub country about 5 km from Wellawaya on the Thanamalwila road, at the south-eastern foot of the highlands
suggested_location.why_here: The site's value is that almost nothing about it is settled, and the one thing that is settled is a number. Seven colossal figures stand cut into one rock face; no ancient text mentions them, nothing inscribed on the rock names them, and every identification and every date on offer is a modern proposal with a proposer's name attached. That is C077's question — an enumeration whose count is exact and argued for — standing in the open at forty feet, with C084's question stacked on it, because the names were all supplied from outside by people the figures never met. It also delivers the cinema the concept needs in the same frame. The wall is reported to face east, so the first hour of light rakes across the relief and lifts seven bodies out of flat grey stone; the central figure is tall enough that one person standing at its foot is the only scale the shot needs; the surviving stucco and the long orange streak give the close work something no reconstruction could; and the surrounding country is empty thorn scrub with a shallow tank in it, so the drone has a subject and the ground camera does not depend on the drone. It is a working temple but not a crowded one, which makes the series' floor keepable here in a way that a major pilgrimage monument would not.
what_to_film: The approach before sunrise: the shallow tank with dead trees standing in the water and birds working the shallows, then the rock wall coming up out of thorn scrub, from the ground and from low height.
The whole face flat on from the ground in the first hour, wide enough to hold all seven with air above the central head, and with nothing in frame that reads as a label or an identification.

The payoff move: tight on the figure nobody has named, pulling steadily back until all seven are in one frame with a single consenting person standing at the foot of the central figure for scale, and the scrub running out to nothing behind.
The robe: the surviving patches of stucco and the long streak of orange, close, in raking light and again after rain when the colour comes up.

The figure that still holds much of its white finish, and the stance of the female figure with her weight thrown into one hip, filmed as carving and framed so that no shot flatters one reading of who they are.
The crevices cut into the rock above the figures, where a roof structure is thought to have been fixed, which is visible evidence that the seven were once meant to be seen in shade.
The flame-shaped hollow at the base of the rock, filmed as it is, with the local account of the oil left in the voice as an account and never as a fact.
The second half of the site: the low foundations and small brick stupa about half a kilometre off in the scrub, for the ending, and the tank at last light.
The wall late in the afternoon in its own shade, as the fallback if the morning is flat and as the closing register either way.
suggested_location.access: By road from the A2 to Wellawaya and then along the Thanamalwila road; published accounts give the turn-off as roughly 5 to 10 km from Wellawaya, followed by a byroad of about 4 km, partly unsealed, to a small car park, and a short walk to the rock. The site is a working temple with a caretaker and a ticket or donation is likely. It is a gazetted archaeological protected monument, notified on 4 June 2004, so the Department of Archaeology governs filming; a drone additionally requires that department's no-objection letter, Ministry of Defence security clearance submitted at least five days ahead, Civil Aviation Authority operating approval on form CAA/AS/017 with third-party insurance, and may be refused over a protected monument regardless. Nothing here can be filmed by turning up.
suggested_location.best_time: The dry months, roughly December to April, when the unsealed section is passable. The first hour after sunrise is the film, on a face reported to be east-facing; late afternoon, with the wall in its own shade, is the second window; the hour after rain is the best the paint traces will look. Avoid poya days and festival days, when the site is in use and the floor cannot be kept.

historical_thread.story: Seven colossal figures are cut in relief out of one face of a rock in low scrub country: a standing Buddha of about thirteen metres in the centre, reported as the tallest standing Buddha figure on the island, with a group of three on its right and a group of three on its left, the flanking figures running between roughly six and seven and a half metres. The central figure stands in the samabhaṅga posture with one hand raised, and still bears traces of its stuccoed robe and a long streak of orange showing that it was once brightly painted; one of the flanking figures keeps much of its white finish. Crevices cut in the rock above the figures suggest a roof structure once covered them. The complex belongs to the Mahāyāna school, which in a largely Theravāda country makes it unusual, and its iconography — a female figure in the thrice-bent posture, a figure holding a vajra, a small meditating Buddha in a headdress — is what the identifications are built on. And that is all the site supplies. No ancient text mentions the place. Nothing carved on the rock names anything on it, and the site's own original name is unknown; the name it now carries is a modern descriptive one meaning the rock of Buddha images. Because there is no text and no inscription, everything else has been argued from style. Senarath Paranavitana proposed the late fifth century and also proposed that the central figure is not Śākyamuni but Dīpaṅkara, pointing among other things to the flame-shaped hollow beside it; Professor Dohanian placed the carvings in the second half of the seventh century; Professor Chandra Wickramagamage placed them in the ninth; other accounts say the tenth, and connect the work to Pallava sculpture of the seventh and eighth centuries. The identifications are equally unsettled. The central figure of one triad is thought to be the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara; the female figure beside him is thought to be Tārā; the third has been called Sudhanakumāra, and Mañjuśrī, and either Vishnu or Brahmā. On the other side a crowned figure is usually called Maitreya and one holding a vajra Vajrapāṇi, while the remaining figure is simply unidentified. In 1916 H. C. P. Bell read one triad not as bodhisattvas at all but as figures from the Vessantara birth story — a brahmin, a king and a queen — and the other as three gods of the local pantheon. About half a kilometre from the carved rock lie the foundations of a ruined monastery with a small stupa and a boundary wall, and a tank lies close by. A hollow cut at the base of the rock, flame-shaped, is reported to be perpetually wet with an oily substance that local accounts say smells of mustard oil, and local legend attaches a sealed treasure chamber to it and blames a broken nose on a colonial hunter. The site was gazetted as a protected monument on 4 June 2004.
historical_thread.how_it_binds: C077 is the compendium of all things, and what it actually does is set out what there is as numbered lists: five aggregates, twelve bases, eighteen elements, four truths. The numbers are not approximate. The Pradeepika argues the order of the five and argues that there are exactly five, neither fewer nor more, and both books say what the counting is for — to loosen the habit of saying I and mine — while the closing passage says the several sortings exist because people are confused about name, about form, or about both. This rock is that practice in stone and in reverse. The count is the one thing about it that has never been in dispute: seven, six and one, checkable from a single frame by anyone. Every name attached to the seven is a scholar's proposal, the proposed dates span five centuries, and there is no text to check any of it against. So the site hands the concept its own question from the other end: what survives when the names go, and what exactly was the name doing? That is where C084 comes in, because a concept in these sources is both what is made known and the means of making it known, and the name-concept is separated from the sound that carries it — the sound being ultimately real, the name living in whoever receives it. A figure in relief was never separated from its rock; it is a configuration of the rock, and the name laid over it is doing all the work of telling anyone what it is. Here the names were supplied a thousand years late, by people whose own names are firmly recorded, to figures that carry none. If this paragraph were a stretch the location would be wrong; it is not a stretch, because the site's central fact is a count that holds and a set of names that do not.
historical_thread.what_is_certain: Seven figures are cut in relief out of one rock face, six flanking one central standing Buddha. The central figure is the tallest standing Buddha figure recorded on the island. It still bears traces of its stuccoed robe and a long streak of orange paint, and one of the flanking figures retains much of its white finish. The complex is of the Mahāyāna school. No ancient text mentions the site and its original name is not known. There is no inscription at the site naming any of the figures. Crevices above the figures indicate a former roof structure. A second part of the site, about half a kilometre away, holds the foundations of a monastery with a small stupa and a boundary wall, and a tank lies nearby. The place was gazetted as a protected monument on 4 June 2004.
historical_thread.what_is_disputed: The date, first. Senarath Paranavitana argued the late fifth century; Professor Dohanian the second half of the seventh; Professor Chandra Wickramagamage the ninth; other published accounts, including the general encyclopaedic ones and several of the reference photographs' own file pages, say the ninth or tenth; and the stylistic connection most often drawn is to Pallava sculpture of the seventh and eighth centuries. Because no ancient text and no inscription refers to the site, all of these rest on style alone. Popular and tourist accounts add attributions that are not scholarly proposals at all — a first-century-BCE king, and in one case an eighteenth-century one — and these are legends rather than datings. Second, the identifications. The central figure is generally taken to be the Buddha, but Paranavitana proposed that it is Dīpaṅkara rather than Śākyamuni, supported by the flame-shaped hollow beside it. The central figure of the triad on the Buddha's right is thought to be the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, on the strength of a small meditating Buddha in his headdress; the female figure beside him, standing in the thrice-bent posture and the only colossal female figure of its kind recorded on the island, is thought to be his consort Tārā; the third figure of that triad is called Sudhanakumāra in some accounts, while others propose Mañjuśrī, and others again either Vishnu or Sahampati Brahmā. In the triad on the Buddha's left, the crowned figure is usually called Maitreya, the figure holding a vajra Vajrapāṇi, and the third is left unidentified, with the same Mañjuśrī, Vishnu and Brahmā proposals circulating for it depending on the account. H. C. P. Bell, writing in 1916, read the seven quite differently: one triad as the brahmin Jūjaka, King Vessantara and Queen Maddī from the Vessantara birth story, and the other as three gods of the local pantheon. Accounts also differ on which triad stands on which side, because some describe the groups from the Buddha's point of view and others from the viewer's, so any voice line must fix its reference frame. Even the measurements are unsettled: the central figure is published as 42 ft 8 in and as 13 m, and also as 15.5 m, 16 m and 51 ft, the last of these on the file pages of photographs used as reference here. The distance from the nearest town is given variously as about 5, 6.4 and 10 km. Finally, the hollow at the base of the rock, its perpetual oil and its smell are reported in local and popular accounts and have no published explanation; they are recorded here as accounts, and the treasure-chamber legend and the story of the broken nose are folklore, not history.

suggested_location.research_note: Desk research only. The seven figures, the relief technique, the Mahāyāna character, the traces of stuccoed robe and the orange streak, the white finish on one flanking figure, the absence of any ancient textual reference, the unknown original name, the rival datings of Paranavitana, Dohanian and Wickramagamage, the Dīpaṅkara proposal, Bell's 1916 reading, the individual heights, the roof crevices, the flame-shaped hollow, the nearby tank, the second site with monastery foundations and a stupa, and the 2004 gazette notification all come from the sources listed above. Coordinates are the decimal form of the 6°41′13″N 81°04′42″E given by Wikipedia and have not been checked against the ground. Three things should be verified before anything is planned around them: the orientation of the rock face, which two sources describe as east-facing and on which the whole first-hour payoff depends; the height of the central figure, which is published variously as 42 ft 8 in, 13 m, 15.5 m, 16 m and 51 ft; and the distance and road condition from the nearest town, given as roughly 5, 6.4 and 10 km in different accounts. The oil in the hollow, the treasure chamber and the broken nose are local and popular accounts, recorded as such. The drone procedure is taken from a current Sri Lankan drone-permit guide and from the Department of Archaeology's role at protected monuments as those sources describe it; none of it has been confirmed with either authority. Six Wikimedia Commons files were verified to exist through the search and query API; note that two of their file pages carry a 16 m height and a tenth-century date, which the film treats as further examples of the disagreement rather than as facts.

unknowns: No permission has been sought or found. Everything here is a research direction, including whether the Department of Archaeology and the temple would allow filming at all.
Drone permission over a gazetted protected monument is unverified and may be refused; the film is built so that it works entirely from the ground if it is.

The orientation of the carved face is reported as east-facing by two secondary sources and has not been confirmed, and the first-hour raking light that the payoff depends on cannot be planned until it is.
Whether the surviving stucco and the orange streak still read on camera at the resolution and distance the film needs, given continued weathering, is unknown.
Whether the flame-shaped hollow at the base is accessible and filmable without touching or disturbing it, and whether the temple regards it as part of the observance, has not been checked.
Whether the ruined monastery foundations half a kilometre away are findable and filmable, or overgrown and off-limits, is unverified.
Whether early-morning movement on foot around the site is advisable, given wild elephant activity in the surrounding dry-zone scrub, has not been checked and would govern the whole dawn schedule.
How busy the site is on an ordinary morning, and therefore whether the floor can be kept while filming the wide frames, is unknown.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location is a research suggestion awaiting Chathura's verdict, and its supporting detail is desk research from published secondary accounts. The historical thread's disputes are recorded as disputes and are not resolved here. No scene or shot is decided.
